entry_points.role: the whole analysis pipeline (314 lines) - the file that matters
despite the name, a RANDOM-sample demo harness (ORDER by random() LIMIT n), not a forecaster

algorithm.detail: nodes = papers; edges from co-citation, bibliographic coupling and direct citation, each stored as a separate attribute
hybrid text similarity = 0.8*cos(embedding) + 0.2*cos(tfidf), each term zeroed below SIMILARITY_TEXT_MIN=0.1, top-(GRAPH_TEXT_SIMILARITY_EDGES=100) neighbours per node
greedy k-nearest-neighbour graph, k=NODE2VEC_GRAPH_EDGES=50, nodes processed by descending degree
node2vec random walks with p=5.0, q=2.0, walk_length=30, walks_per_node=50, seed=42, then gensim Word2Vec(vector_size=64, window=5, sg=1, epochs=3)
AgglomerativeClustering when n_papers <= MAX_AGGLOMERATIVE_CLUSTERING=5000 else KMeans; labels renumbered by descending cluster size

per-cluster token frequency vectors normalised to unit length; score = (unit vector entry for that cluster) * log1p(total token count); top n_words taken. Picks words whose frequency profile is closest to one-hot for the cluster.
top cited; per-year absolute max gain; per-year relative gain = citations_this_year / cumulative_before (guarded at 0 -> 1), reported when >= 0.01

temporal_behaviour.evidence: every module in pysrc/papers/analysis operates on a single current result set; there is no holdout, no lagged target and no scored prediction anywhere in the repository. 'predict_analyzer.py' samples a random PMID subset for demo purposes.
temporal_behaviour.implication: 'topic change and emerging research areas' are rendered as per-cluster paper counts by publication year, not as forecasts.

reproduction.classification_reason: PubTrends publishes no forecasting accuracy number to reproduce, and its stack is forbidden to deploy. The reproduction therefore reimplements and unit-checks the distinctive algorithms in pure Python on synthetic inputs, and records the two upstream defects that the checks exposed.

checks.what: node2vec p/q transition probabilities equal the 1/p, 1, 1/q rule (analytic vs 200k sampled walks)
heavier edge gets proportionally higher probability
k-NN sparsification: edges are top-k for >=1 endpoint, but the degree cap is NOT strict
topic description recovers cluster-specific tokens and demotes a shared high-frequency token
absolute max-gain correct; relative 'hot paper' gain exceeds 1.0 in a paper's first citation year
no held-out predictive evaluation exists in the repository

upstream_defects_found.detail: with k=5 on a synthetic 120-node graph, 18 nodes ended with degree 6-7 (max 7). The greedy loop gates insertion on the PEER's degree (len(result.neighbors(x)) < k) but never checks the current node's own degree before adding its own k edges, so a node that already received edges as a peer can overshoot up to ~2k-1. In production this runs with k=50.
upstream_defects_found.evidence: pt_results.json check C; diagnosed on a 120-node / 1051-edge random weighted graph

upstream_defects_found.detail: the denominator is cumulative citations BEFORE the year with a guard replacing 0 by 1, so in a paper's first citation year the metric equals the raw count and can exceed 1.0 (measured 10.0 for a paper with 10 first-year citations). The >=0.01 reporting threshold therefore always admits newly-cited papers, biasing the 'hot paper per year' view.

not_attempted: full stack (forbidden: Postgres + Redis + Celery + Flask)
end-to-end analysis on real PubMed/S2 data (terabyte-scale corpora)
gensim Word2Vec embedding itself (checked only the walk-transition mathematics that feeds it)

limitations: an exploration/dashboard product, not a predictive method: nothing to reproduce against
requires PostgreSQL + pgvector + Redis + Celery; heavy operational surface for any reuse
datasets are terabyte-scale and cannot be exercised within the audit budget
~48 of 52 Python dependencies are unpinned, so the exact analysis stack is not reproducible
algorithm parameters (p/q, similarity weights, k, thresholds) are hardcoded constants with no calibration evidence in the repo
cluster labels are recomputed per query and are not comparable across time, which undercuts any 'topic change' reading
leakage_risks: no point-in-time discipline: a search result set is clustered using all papers returned, including papers published after whatever date the user is reasoning about. Any 'this area was emerging in year Y' claim built from a present-day query leaks the future.
cumulative citation counts are contemporaneous; using total citations to rank 'impact' or 'hot' topics is look-ahead if used as a leading indicator
the relative-gain 'hot paper' metric is biased towards papers in their first citation year (see defect F), so it does not measure acceleration
cluster identity is not stable over time or across queries, so 'topic X grew' is not a defined statement in this architecture
KMeans with no fixed seed in cluster_and_sort (unlike node2vec's seed=42) makes cluster membership non-deterministic for >5000-paper result sets

overlaps: literature/publication signal intake (MedRadar has pysrc OpenAlex publication counts in medradar/intelligence/sources/publications.py)
paper-level metadata and graph construction (MedRadar tkg + graph_context)
does_not_overlap: topic clustering of a downloaded literature set
capability_overlap_with_medradar.medradar_gap_it_could_fill: no current component clusters a paper set into labelled topics; PubTrends' topic-description trick would be the portable part

decision.reason: licence is clean (Apache-2.0, so reuse is legally unproblematic) and the project is well maintained, but it is an exploration web service with no temporal model, no train/test protocol and no predictive metric - there is no method to adopt for MedRadar's forecasting lane. Its two genuinely reusable pieces (one-hot-cosine topic description, composite-similarity kNN graph) are ~150 lines that would be cheaper to reimplement under our own tests than to integrate, and deploying the Postgres/Redis/Faiss stack is both forbidden here and disproportionate to the value.
